title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
description: Some nights the Moon is a big round ball. Other nights it is a thin smile. The Moon itself never changes shape — what changes is how much of its sunny side we can see.

body.heading: The Moon does not make its own light
paragraphs: The Moon is like a big ball floating in space. It does not glow by itself. The Sun shines on it, just like a lamp shines on a ball. The side facing the Sun is bright. The other side is dark.
We only see the Moon because sunlight bounces off it and comes back to our eyes. The bright light we call moonlight is really sunlight, taking a little trip to the Moon and back.

body.heading: So why does it look different each night?
paragraphs: The Moon travels around the Earth, and as it moves, we see a different amount of its bright side. When we can see the whole bright side, we call it a full moon. When we see only a little sliver, we call it a crescent moon. In between come the half moon and the fat, almost-round moon.

These shapes have names, and they follow each other in order, over and over. It takes about 29 and a half days to go from one new moon to the next new moon — almost a whole month. That is why we can watch the Moon grow from a smile to a ball, then shrink back to a smile again.

body.heading: Try it with a lamp and a ball
paragraphs: With an adult, go into a dark room. The adult holds a lamp still — that is the Sun. You hold a ball out in front of you — that is the Moon. Now turn around slowly, in a circle. Watch the ball: sometimes you see its bright side, sometimes only a little edge, and sometimes it looks dark. You are seeing moon phases, right in your own room.

takeaway: The Moon never changes shape — we just see a different amount of its sunny side each night.
supervision: An adult guides the torch-and-ball demonstration and stays with the child throughout.
